Rick Steves' Picks

Top Sites in Ghent

Ghent offers cobbled streets, centuries-old architecture, and canals that glow with beautiful uplighting at night — plus just the right mix of grittiness and creativity. Here are the must-sees for your family.

Square & Bridge tap to expand
City Center

Korenmarkt & St. Michael's Bridge

The Grain Market square (Korenmarkt) is the historic heart of Ghent, once so large and prosperous it didn't have just one Great Market — it had many specialized squares for different trades. A short walk leads to St. Michael's Bridge, the best 360-degree panorama in Ghent: three towers visible in one view, guild houses along the canal, and the Castle of the Counts in the distance.

📸 Best Photo Spot: From St. Michael's Bridge you can see all three of Ghent's iconic towers at once — St. Nicholas, the dragon-topped Belfry, and St. Bavo's spire. The guild houses along the canal glow beautifully at night.
🏛️ What's that prickly medieval-looking building near the square? ▾
It's the former post office, now a ritzy shopping complex. Despite looking medieval, it was actually completed in 1910 in Neo-Gothic and Neo-Renaissance style. Over the entrance you'll find symbols glorifying Belgium, Flanders, Wallonia, and the Belgian Congo. On the side, there's even a bust of Florence Nightingale!
Waterfront tap to expand
Along the Leie River

Korenlei

The Korenlei ("Grain Quay") is one of Ghent's most picturesque stretches — a canal embankment lined with ornately decorated guild houses that once served as meeting halls and warehouses for Ghent's boatmen, grain traders, and weighers. This is where the city's medieval commerce came to life, with goods arriving from across Europe. Today the quayside is a favorite spot for strolling and canal boat tours.

🚤 Hop a Boat: Tourist boats depart along this embankment, giving you a water-level view of Ghent's guild houses and medieval skyline — one of the best ways to see the city and a great rest from walking.
🌙 Why does this stretch look so magical at night? ▾
Ghent spent years on a city-wide design project to install thoughtful uplighting along its canals and historic buildings. The Korenlei and the facing Graslei embankment are among the most dramatic results — guild house facades glow warmly against the dark water, creating reflections that make this one of the most photographed nighttime scenes in all of Belgium.
Castle tap to expand
Sint-Veerleplein

Castle of the Counts (Gravensteen)

Built in 1180 by Philip of Alsace, this rough-stone fortress was modeled on the Krak des Chevaliers in Syria — which Philip visited during the Crusades. It wasn't built to protect the citizens of Ghent; it was built to intimidate them. Today you can explore the full castle including towers, dungeons, ramparts, and displays of real swords and armor. An audio guide narrated by a Belgian comedian makes it genuinely fun.

🏰 Don't Miss: Climb to the top of a tower for sweeping views over Ghent. Find the room where prisoners awaited their fate — punishments were very literal (thieves lost their hands; those who insulted the count lost their tongues).
🪢 Why is there a noose beer in Ghent? ▾
In 1540, Holy Roman Emperor Charles V demanded a massive tribute from the city. When citizens refused, he came personally to crush the rebellion. The city leaders had to pay — and then beg forgiveness on their knees, with nooses around their necks. Today Ghent's most popular local beer is called 't Stropke ("The Noose"), and locals are affectionately nicknamed "noose bearers" (Stroppedragers).
Hidden Gem tap to expand
Hoogpoort area

Graffitistraatje (Graffiti Lane)

This narrow passageway once drained rainwater away from the high ground between Ghent's two rivers. Today it has a very different purpose. Instead of banning graffiti entirely, the city designated this single street as a legal outlet for street artists — a typically pragmatic Belgian solution. The result is a constantly rotating open-air gallery.

🌿 Hidden Garden: Halfway down the lane, look for a beautiful fenced-in garden on your right. This city-owned green space is open to the public — few tourists know it's there.
🎨 Is there a way to take home the art? ▾
There may even be a small shop along the lane selling works by the artists who paint here. The artwork changes constantly, so what you see on your visit will be unique to your trip. No two visits to Graffitistraatje are exactly alike.
Historic Building tap to expand
Hoogpoort & Botermarkt

Ghent City Hall (Stadhuis)

Ghent's grand City Hall was a prestigious symbol of self-rule — a monument to the special privileges the city had negotiated from the counts of Flanders. The ornate Gothic core along Hoogpoort dates from the early 16th century, while the Neoclassical section with black-and-gold columns on Botermarkt was added a century later, following the architectural fashion of the day.

🏛️ Two Buildings in One: Walk around both sides and you'll see two completely different architectural styles stitched together — Gothic grandeur meets Neoclassical order. It's a great example of how Ghent kept building onto things rather than tearing them down.
📜 Why was this building such a big deal in medieval Ghent? ▾
Ghent had negotiated a remarkable degree of self-governance from the counts of Flanders in exchange for financial support. The City Hall was the physical embodiment of that independence — a place where Ghent ran its own affairs. This freedom made the city wealthy and proud, but also put it on a collision course with rulers like Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, who crushed a Ghent rebellion in 1540.
Tower tap to expand
Sint-Baafsplein

Belfry of Ghent (Belfort)

Standing since the 14th century, the Belfry was originally built to house and protect Ghent's charter of privileges, granted by the counts of Flanders. The Neo-Gothic spire was added when Ghent hosted the World's Fair in 1913. You can go inside and ride an elevator most of the way up for views over the city.

🐉 Look Up: See the golden dragon at the very top? It's not a symbol of evil — it's a protector who never sleeps, watching over the city's rights. The original 1380 dragon is on display inside at Level 0. Can you spot the four sentinels at the tower's corners?
🎵 When does the tower play music? ▾
A carillon plays a tune every 15 minutes and a longer piece at the top of every hour (often a Belgian popular song). Free concerts on Sunday mornings year-round from 11:00–12:00, and Saturday evenings in July and August. Ask locally for exact times.
🔔 What will you see inside? ▾
Level 0: original dragons and spire models. Level 1: a bell museum with a film about how bells are cast. Level 2: the giant bell called "Roland." Level 3: a rotating drum that programs carillon melodies — like a giant music box! Plus a gorgeous painting of medieval Ghent in the main hall.
Square tap to expand
Sint-Baafsplein

St. Bavo's Square

This lively square in front of the cathedral became a symbolic battleground between Belgium's Dutch-speaking and French-speaking communities during the 1800s and 1900s. The ornate Dutch Theater (built 1899) gave the city's Dutch speakers their own stage — a proud cultural statement at a time when French-speaking elites dominated Belgian society.

🦁 Look at the Statue: The muscular figure in the center celebrates the resurrection of the Dutch language. Notice the Flemish lion on their flag. The relief on the base honors Jan Frans Willems, a founder of the Flemish cultural revival movement.
⚡ What did a power company owner do to protest Dutch at the university? ▾
When Ghent's university was finally allowed to teach in Dutch instead of French and Latin, a French-speaking industrialist who owned the local electric company cut power to the city in protest — plunging Ghent into darkness to mourn what he saw as a rejection of "enlightened thinking." It took a full century of advocacy before the change was made.
🍫 What's worth seeing near the theater? ▾
Just to the left of the theater is Chocolatier Van Hoorebeke, a producer of fine Belgian pralines. Look through the glass floor inside the shop to watch the chocolate makers working below — a surprisingly cool and interactive peek behind the scenes of one of Belgium's most beloved crafts.
Cathedral tap to expand
Sint-Baafsplein

St. Bavo's Cathedral

Ghent's Gothic cathedral has a jaw-dropping 292-foot tower and a history that includes baptizing Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. Inside is a beautifully carved Rococo pulpit, a Rubens altar painting, and — in its own darkened chapel — the breathtaking Ghent Altarpiece. Built from around 1350 to 1559 on the site of structures going back to the year 942.

🎨 The Main Event: The Van Eyck altarpiece gets its own section on this page — it's that important. Even before you go inside, take a moment to look up at the 292-foot tower. It takes some serious neck-craning!
🪨 What do the different building materials tell you? ▾
Red brick in the nave walls, yellow stone in the pillars, and gray stone in the choir — each material tells a story about when that section was built and how wealthy Ghent was at the time. The same economic story shows up in the Church of St. Nicholas across the square: the most expensive stone was used first, when Ghent was richest.
🎭 Who is St. Bavo, and why is he the patron saint of TWO cities? ▾
St. Bavo was a 7th-century Ghent nobleman who was once a wealthy, rambunctious young soldier. After his wife died, he had a change of heart, rejected his materialistic life, and became a hermit-monk — reportedly living for a time in a hollow tree. He's the patron saint of both Ghent and Haarlem in the Netherlands.
Church tap to expand
Korenmarkt

Church of St. Nicholas (Sint-Niklaaskerk)

Built mostly in the 13th century during a boom time for Ghent, this church was the favorite of the river traders who sold goods at the nearby Grain Market. It's a textbook example of Scheldt Gothic style: bluish-gray stone, turrets, and a single central tower. Inside, look for the very Baroque altar with corkscrew columns and a 19th-century organ.

🪨 Stone Detective: Bluish-gray limestone = Ghent at its wealthy peak (before 1400). Yellow sandstone = economy slowing (1400–1500). Red brick = hard times after 1500. See if you can find all three as you walk around!
🔨 What happened to all the original art inside? ▾
In the 16th century, Calvinist Protestants ("iconoclasts") stormed Catholic churches and stripped them of all decorations, which they saw as idolatrous. Almost all medieval art in Ghent's churches was destroyed. The modern stained glass above represents the seven sacraments, replacing what was lost.
Inside St. Bavo's

Parts of St. Bavo's Cathedral

St. Bavo's isn't just one big room — it's a collection of stunning spaces, each with its own story. Here's a guide to what you'll find as you explore this Gothic masterpiece.

🏙️
Exterior Tower

At 292 feet tall, the tower is the tallest structure in Ghent. Look up from the square and crane your neck — really crane it. The church was built between about 1350 and 1559 on a site that has had a religious building since the year 942.

🏛️
The Nave

The main hall soars to a 100-foot-high ceiling with Gothic arches and stained glass. Notice three materials: red brick walls, yellow stone pillars, and gray stone in the choir. All interior decorations and stained glass date from the 19th century — the originals were destroyed by iconoclasts in the 1500s.

🎤
Rococo Pulpit

Carved in the 1740s from white stone and wood with golden highlights, this extraordinary pulpit depicts the Tree of Life and Tree of Knowledge. Look for the marble woman with a sun on her bosom waking up "Time," the winged old man — a Counter-Reformation message to wake up to the Catholic faith. Two cheeky angels at the staircases watch the congregation.

🙏
Statue of St. Bavo

Above the main altar, this 7th-century saint appears to be ascending to heaven. Once a wealthy, hard-living young soldier, Bavo turned his life around after his wife died — eventually becoming a hermit-monk who reportedly lived in a hollow tree. He's the patron saint of both Ghent and Haarlem, Netherlands.

🎨
The Rubens Painting

Peter Paul Rubens' "St. Bavo Entering the Monastery of Ghent" (1624) shows the dramatic moment the former soldier-turned-saint begins his new life. Rubens painted himself as Bavo in the red cloak. Below, his estate manager distributes belongings to the poor. The two women are modeled after Rubens' two actual wives — spot the difference in how he portrays them!

🧑‍⚕️
Pater Damiaan Chapel

On your way up the right aisle, pause at the second chapel for a statue of Father Damien (1840–1889) — a Flemish missionary who sailed to Hawaii to care for people with leprosy. After 16 years, he died of leprosy himself. He was made a saint in 2009 and is an important figure to both Belgians and Hawaiians.

🖼️
The Altarpiece Chapel

The showstopper: the Ghent Altarpiece lives in its own darkened chapel, meticulously restored and presented all by itself. This is where modern oil painting was born. This is where kings, conquerors, and Nazis came to steal a potent symbol of civilization. See a full section of this guide for the full story.

⛏️
Building Materials

Like a detective clue, the stone tells Ghent's economic story: gray stone in the choir (the most valuable area, built when money flowed), yellow sandstone in the pillars (transitional period), and red brick in the nave walls (later, more economical times). Three materials, three eras, one building.

Belgium's Greatest Art Mystery

The Ghent Altarpiece: Coveted, Looted, Stolen, Lost

The Adoration of the Mystic Lamb — painted by Jan van Eyck and his brother Hubert — is widely considered the greatest art treasure in Ghent, and possibly in all of Belgium. It's a monumental masterpiece where modern oil painting was essentially born. But its story isn't just about art. It's an action-packed thriller spanning six centuries.

The altarpiece has been stolen or looted at least six times, making it perhaps the most stolen painting in all of history. Invaders ranging from kings to Napoleon to the Nazis have coveted it. And to this day, one panel remains missing. Here's the full timeline:

Today: except for one panel (a high-quality copy stands in its place), the altarpiece is fully restored and on display in its own darkened chapel in St. Bavo's. It is genuinely breathtaking in person.

1566
The Iconoclasts Protestant iconoclasts stormed St. Bavo's, determined to burn the altarpiece as a symbol of Catholic idolatry. Fortunately, priests had hidden it safely at the top of the cathedral tower just in time.
1794
Napoleon Takes Four Panels Napoleon carried off the four central paintings as war trophies and displayed them in the Louvre in Paris from 1794 to 1815.
1821
Smuggled to Germany The King of Prussia smuggled several panels to Germany. The art was so valued internationally that the Treaty of Versailles (ending World War I) specifically ordered Germany to return them.
1934
The Just Judges — Still Missing Someone broke into St. Bavo's and stole the "Just Judges" panel. The thief — possibly a Flemish banker — died saying only he knew where it was hidden. The panel has never been found.
WWII
Nazis vs. Monuments Men Hitler coveted the altarpiece as a symbol of Teutonic art supremacy. The Nazis discovered it hidden in the French Pyrenees and moved it to a Bavarian castle, then an Austrian salt mine. At war's end, the "Monuments Men" — Allied art preservationists — tracked it down and returned it home.
2008
The Parking Garage Search20 Ghent police officers tore up 225 square feet of a parking garage looking for the missing Just Judges panel, following a tip from an amateur sleuth. It came up empty. A 2015 tip was also deemed not credible.
From Powerhouse to Living City

Ghent Through the Ages

Once one of the biggest cities in Europe — rivaling Paris itself — Ghent's story is one of staggering wealth, dramatic decline, and gradual rebirth as a vibrant university city.

942
The Earliest Structures
The site where St. Bavo's Cathedral now stands already had religious buildings here. Ghent was founded at the confluence of two rivers — the Lys and the Scheldt — giving it a natural geographic advantage for trade.
1180
Castle of the Counts
Philip of Alsace builds the Gravensteen — modeled after a Syrian crusader castle. It's designed not to protect the citizens of Ghent, but to keep them in line. The city's textile wealth is already making it politically complicated to govern.
1300s
Peak of Power
Ghent's population reaches 65,000 — enormous for the era. Two-thirds of the city are textile workers. North of the Alps, only Paris is larger. Ghent is arguably Europe's first industrial city, thriving on the wool trade and weaving high-fashion cloth for export across Europe.
1432
The Van Eyck Altarpiece
Jan van Eyck and his brother Hubert complete the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb for St. Bavo's. This landmark work is considered the birthplace of modern oil painting technique and becomes one of the most celebrated works of art in history.
1500
Birth of an Emperor
Holy Roman Emperor Charles V is born in Ghent and baptized in St. Bavo's Cathedral. He would become one of the most powerful people in all of Europe — yet he would later come back personally to crush a Ghent rebellion and humiliate its leaders.
1500s
Decline Begins
Competition from Brussels and England, combined with a conservative guild leadership slow to adapt, causes Ghent's economy to collapse. The Reformation arrives, and iconoclasts strip the city's churches of their medieval art. The city's glory days are over — but its architecture remains.
Today
A Living Medieval City
Home to one of Belgium's biggest universities and a vibrant student population, Ghent has reinvented itself. The historic quarter still looks much as it did circa 1500. Cobbled streets, uplighting on the canals, creative hipster culture, and world-class shopping give it a unique energy. It's the kind of city where you plan a few hours and wish you had a few days.
Did You Know?

Interesting Facts about Ghent

These are the details that tend to get overlooked — but they're some of the best stories Ghent has to offer. Tap to reveal each answer.

🎭
The Dutch Theater on St. Bavo's Square has a golden mosaic above the entrance. What does it show — and why?
The mosaic depicts Apollo returning to Mount Parnassus. It was chosen deliberately: just as Apollo was returning home, the Flemish people felt they were finally coming home to their ancestral Dutch language, after generations of being governed by French-speaking elites who treated Dutch as inferior.
🔥
The Belfry wasn't just a tower for storing city documents. What important safety role did it play for medieval Ghent?
The Belfry served as a fire watchtower for the city. The four stone sentries positioned at the corners of the tower represent this role — each one standing guard, watching over the city below for signs of fire. In a medieval city built largely of wood, an early warning could mean the difference between a small fire and a catastrophe.
🏗️
There's a large building attached to the base of the Belfry that most visitors walk right past. What was it, and why did it matter?
It's the Cloth Hall, and it was central to Ghent's entire reason for existing. This is where the city's textile merchants conducted business — buying, selling, and trading the woven cloth that made Ghent one of the wealthiest cities in medieval Europe. Without the cloth trade, there would have been no money to build the Belfry, the cathedral, or the castle.
👩‍⚕️
There's a famous Victorian-era English nurse commemorated on the side of a building in the middle of Ghent's historic center. Who is she, and why is she there?
Florence Nightingale — the pioneering nurse who transformed medical care during the Crimean War — has a bust on the side of the former post office building near Korenmarkt. The building's decorations celebrate the leaders of all nations who joined the International Postal Union, and its window friezes include the coats of arms of every Belgian province and major city.
⚔️
Philip of Alsace built the Castle of the Counts in 1180. But why did it take so long for him and his wife to actually live there?
Philip and his wife married as teenagers, but they didn't settle in Ghent until they were nearly 40. In the years between, Philip had gone off on the Second Crusade — visiting the Middle East, where he saw the fortress that would inspire the design of his own castle back home. The Krak des Chevaliers in Syria was the model for what became the Gravensteen.
